opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to look a lot less dramatic than people imagine. There won't be a moment where some company announces that an AI is now the CEO and everyone suddenly realizes AIs can manage. It'll be much more gradual and much more boring.

What I expect is that AIs will first take over pieces of what managers do: scheduling, allocating tasks, monitoring progress, writing performance summaries, deciding which tickets go to which engineer. A lot of management is coordination and information processing, and those parts are relatively easy to hand off. People will start delegating more and more of that, often without thinking of it as "AI managing" at all. They'll just think of it as a tool that makes the manager more productive.

The harder parts are the long-horizon judgment calls: what to prioritize over the next year, how to handle a team that's not working well, when to cut losses on a project. Those require agency and coherence over long time periods, and I think current systems are still quite weak there. So I'd expect that to come later, and to be recognized mostly through competitive pressure rather than through anyone deciding to trust AI in principle.

Concretely, you'd see some firms lean much more heavily on AI for these decisions, maybe out of necessity, maybe because they're small and can't afford many managers. If those firms consistently outperform, others copy them. That's how most organizational innovations spread historically. Nobody proved in advance that the assembly line or modern accounting practices were better; firms that adopted them just did better, and the market selected for them.

There's also a legal and social layer. Even when an AI is effectively making the decisions, you'll probably have a human nominally in charge for a long time, because someone has to be accountable, sign contracts, and be liable. So formal recognition will lag the actual capability, possibly by quite a lot. By the time it's officially acknowledged that AIs are managing, they'll likely have been doing much of the real work for years.

r001.rationale: It says formal recognition will lag actual capability, possibly by quite a lot, after AIs have already done much of the management work for years.

r002.rationale: It describes managers gradually delegating workflow tasks to AI because it makes them more productive, with successful firms prompting others to copy the practice.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it'll be recognized the same way most capabilities get recognized, which is not through some clean demonstration but through people gradually noticing that the thing works and that it's cheaper than the alternative. So the way I'd picture it is, first you get AI systems being used as something like a very capable assistant or chief of staff to a human manager. The human is nominally making the decisions, but increasingly the AI is the one tracking everything, drafting the plans, flagging the problems, deciding what the human should be looking at. And at some point the human notices that when they override the AI's recommendation, things tend to go worse on average, and when they go along with it, things go better.

And that's actually a very different kind of evidence than what you get from a benchmark. Benchmarks are good for things like coding or math, where you can check the answer. Management is hard to benchmark because the outcomes are noisy, they take a long time to materialize, and there's a lot of counterfactual uncertainty. You can't easily run the same company twice. So I'd expect the recognition to come from something more like the adoption data: firms that lean on AI for coordination and resource allocation and hiring decisions start outperforming the ones that don't, and that shows up in the usual way, through competition. The firms that don't adopt either copy the ones that do, or they lose market share.

I think there's also a question of what "management" even means here, because a lot of what managers do is really about handling the limitations of humans. You have to break tasks down into pieces because no single person can hold the whole thing in their head, you have to deal with motivation and communication overhead and people leaving. If you have AI systems doing a lot of the underlying work, some of those problems just go away, and the management task changes shape. So in some sense AI might get recognized as good at management partly because the kind of management that's needed becomes something AI is naturally suited to, rather than AI becoming good at the thing a human middle manager does today.

The one caveat I'd give is that I think this could lag the underlying capability by quite a bit. There are trust issues, there are liability issues, there's the fact that a lot of organizations are quite slow to change how they operate. So I wouldn't be surprised if AI systems are competent at a lot of managerial tasks for a while before that's widely acknowledged. But I'd expect the gap to close, and I'd expect it to close fastest in domains where the feedback is quickest, so something like running a software project or an online business before something like running a large government agency.

r001.rationale: The response says recognition may lag underlying capability “by quite a bit,” with systems competent at managerial tasks before they are widely acknowledged.

r002.rationale: It describes AI first assisting human managers in their work, managers noticing that following its recommendations improves outcomes, and firms adopting it as those benefits become apparent.

astra-6.text:
I think it will probably happen gradually, through people delegating more and more of their work to AI. You start by asking it to do some fairly well-defined task. Then you find that it can also break a larger project into smaller tasks, decide what needs to happen first, and check whether the results are any good. At that point, you're already giving it some of the responsibilities of a manager, even if you don't call it that.

The interesting step is when an AI can coordinate work better than the person supervising it. Maybe it notices that a project is stuck because two people are making incompatible assumptions, or that a team is spending time on something that isn't actually necessary. If it reliably catches those things and helps projects succeed, people have a reason to give it more authority.

But I would distinguish being able to give convincing management advice from actually being a good manager. The evidence has to come from outcomes over time. I expect recognition to come first in areas where those outcomes are relatively easy to observe, and then spread as people become more comfortable delegating.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts gradual recognition, but does not say recognition may substantially lag the emergence of the capability.

r002.rationale: It describes people gradually delegating more work and granting AI more authority when its management contributions help projects succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect it to happen gradually, through people delegating more of their work to AI. Initially, you might ask an AI to do a fairly specific task. But as it becomes more capable, you can give it a broader objective, and it starts breaking that objective into smaller tasks, deciding what to prioritize, and checking whether the results are any good. Those are already management functions, even if nobody calls them that.

The interesting transition is when the AI becomes better at deciding what should be done than the person supervising it. You might still have a human manager formally responsible, but increasingly they're approving plans that the AI has developed. At some point, people notice that the teams or businesses operating this way perform better, and the organizational structure starts to reflect that.

I’m less sure how quickly this happens with managing people, because there are issues of trust and legitimacy. Managing other AI systems could be a much more straightforward route. An AI coordinating a large number of other AIs could demonstrate quite substantial management ability before we see companies appointing AI managers over human employees.

r001.rationale: The response says AI already performs management functions before people call them that, but it does not clearly say recognition may lag substantially.

r002.rationale: It describes people delegating more work to AI, managers approving AI-developed plans, and people noticing better performance in organizations that use this approach.
